newsitem.title: USA: Faro will help push lead into surplus - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Faro will help push lead into surplus - analysts.

text.p: The widely-expected start-up of Anvil Range Mining Corp's Faro lead/zinc mine later this year will help create bigger than expected concentrates surpluses and cap the price of lead in particular, analysts said.

"I don't think either concentrates markets needs additional production at this time," analyst Claire Hassall of Brook Hunt said. "We were looking for a surplus in both markets next year, so it will just be even bigger."
Adam Rowley of Macquarie Equities said even with Faro starting up, zinc metal, as opposed to concentrates, was still expected to remain in deficit of 100,000 tonnes next year.
"The impact on lead will be far greater than for zinc," Rowley said.
Lead will be hammered more than zinc because a Faro start up would coincide with BHP's new Cannington lead/silver mine in Australia coming on stream, analysts said.
Cannington will produce 165,000 tonnes of contained lead in concentrates annually.
Analyst David Cook of Lake Engineering said demand for lead was growing but the Anvil start-up, coupled with Cannington would affect lead prices.
"It will probably put a cap on where the lead price is going, and that could occur towards the end of this year or the first quarter of next year," Cook said.
Rowley expected the lead metal market to move into a surplus of 20,000 tonnes of next year compared with an expected small deficit in 1997.

Zinc recently soared to 6-3/4 year highs as London Metal Exchange stocks shrink and tightness looms. Higher prices could encourage more marginal mines to restart and smelters with spare capacity to step up output, analysts said.
On Monday Anvil said it agreed in principle with 27.7 percent owner Cominco Ltd for a C$15 million secured loan to fund a stripping program at its Grum ore deposit in Faro, Yukon, Canada.
Stripping was needed to prepare the mine for resumption of full scale operations, Anvil said. The mine was shut last December because of weak lead and zinc prices.
In the 14 months ended December 31, 1996 Faro produced 345,700 tonnes of zinc concentrates and 186,000 tonnes of lead concentrates.

Just as the closure of Faro last December helped set the scene for miners to wrest lower concentrates treatment charges from smelters, Faro's start up along with Cannington, will strengthen the smelters' hand to secure higher treatment charges next year, analysts said.

In addition, primary lead smelters are already using more lead scrap mixed with their concentrate feed, but scrap units could be pushed out if there is an abundance of cheaper concentrates, some observers argued.
"The benefits of using scrap will diminish next year as more and more concentrates come on and the treatment charge will be expected to increase as a result," Rowley said.
